steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn never sounded on its own. Elias Harper knew every creak and sigh of the lantern room, every mood of the sea, and the foghorn was as dependable as the tides: it called only when he pulled the lever.

Yet on the night of the second storm, it bellowed before he even reached the stairs.

He had been at the kitchen table, oiling the brass of his pocket watch, listening to the slow tick that divided his days into small, familiar pieces. The first storm had passed that morning, leaving the stones slick and the air raw. Nothing in the sky suggested another was coming, only lines of thin clouds and a pale, indifferent moon.

Then the horn’s low moan rolled through the old stones of Greyhook Light.

It came once, long and shuddering, as if the tower itself were groaning. Elias froze, watch in one hand, rag in the other. A second call followed, shorter, impatient. The lamp overhead trembled in its hook.

“Now that’s not right,” he murmured.

He set the watch on the table, careful even in his sudden unease, and climbed.

The spiral steps wound upward in a narrow throat of stone. He knew each turn, each cold patch of wall, each notch worn smooth by his hand over decades. The horn called again, closer to a human cry the longer it echoed.

Halfway up, he saw the first sign something was wrong: a faint strand of water seeping down the inner wall, glimmering in the lamplight. The sea was on the other side of twenty feet of rock and mortar. It did not seep.

At the service level, the air changed. It smelled of wet metal and salt, but also something else: ozone, like the breath of lightning in a closed room. The horn called again, and Elias stepped into the lantern room.

The great lens stood in the center, a glass cathedral of concentric rings. The lamp at its heart burned with a steady, golden flame. Beyond it, the night sky spread in a clear black bowl, pricked by stars. No storm clouds. No rain on the windows. The horizon-line was sharp as a blade.

But the horn control lever, a black iron arm near the bank of instruments, was moving.

It shivered in its housing, clicked, then ratcheted downward. The horn sounded as it did only when called upon, a long, low blast that seemed to pull at his chest. Then the lever snapped back up as though an invisible hand had released it.

Elias watched, feeling the slow pound of his heart in his ears. He walked closer, boots scraping the stone floor, the lamp’s light tracing long shadows across the brass fittings. He said nothing. The tower knew his voice too well; if he spoke into this wrongness, he might give it roots.

The lever twitched again.

He laid calloused fingers on the metal. It was cold. When the mechanism tried to pull down, it jerked under his palm like a living thing. It wanted to sound the horn.

He held it steady.

“Enough of that,” he muttered, more out of habit than certainty. “I’m the one gives warning, not you.”

The pressure eased. The lever stopped.

For a long minute he stood there, the horn silent, the flame whispering faintly. Beyond the glass, the sea lay down in darkness, a dim sheen where the moon touched it.

Elias had been keeper of Greyhook for thirty-two years. Before him, his father. Before that, an uncle he could barely remember, his face obscured by the bright edge of childhood memory. The light had always belonged to his family. That was what the Service liked: continuity, a known eye watching the coast.

But the sea did not care about continuity, and sometimes he suspected the tower did not either.

Downstairs, in the keeper’s office, the logbook waited on its shelf: a spine of cracked leather holding weather, ship names, repairs, dates, small complaints. There was a column for “Unusual Occurrence,” printed in ink that had long faded to a ghost of brown.

He had written in that column only three times.

The first had been his father’s entry: Lights observed at sea behaving contrary to known vessels. The second, his own, fifteen years ago: Apparent voice heard within lantern room when alone. No source found.

The third, two nights ago: Foghorn responded ten seconds before I pulled lever. No visible cause. Weather clear.

The inspector in the city would see those notes once a year, purse his lips, and mutter something about aging equipment, strange acoustics, tricks of the dark. Elias never argued. The explanations stayed on the mainland. Here, at Greyhook, there was only the light, the sea, and the long, thin thread of duty that tied him between them.

He kept his hand on the lever a little longer, until he was sure the mechanism would behave. Then he did what he had always done: climbed the last few steps to the lamp, checked the wick, adjusted the vents. Routine was a rope he had learned to coil around his own anxiety.

By the time he finished, the clock in the hall below struck midnight. The sound reached him in thin, metallic notes.

The horn, blessedly, stayed quiet.

He made one slow circuit of the lantern room, checking the windows, the rails, the anchor points. There were faint traces of moisture on the inner glass, dew that should not have formed on this side, beads of water clinging as though a cloud had passed through.

His fingertips brushed one droplet. It was warm.

He wiped it off on his sleeve and turned a slow circle, looking for the storm no one else could see.

On the horizon, a light moved.

He almost dismissed it as a fishing boat. The local crews liked to run their nets at night, dragging yellow lamps like low stars. But this light was wrong. It was too high above the water, too still amid the small swells he knew must be there. It stood, a fixed point of pale blue-white on a seam in the darkness where no buoy or ship should be.

Elias stepped closer to the glass. The lens refracted and multiplied the glow, long thin ribs of light slicing the night. He narrowed his eyes, squinting past the distortions.

The light blinked.

Not a random flicker from a lantern in the wind, not the steady code of another lighthouse, but a pattern: three short, three long, three short. Then a pause. Then again.

His first thought, absurd and immediate, was of a child calling his name.

The lamp’s flame hummed softly in its housing. The wind pressed against the glass and was turned aside. The horn waited under his hand, silent but not at rest.

Elias reached for the drawer built into the small desk near the chart table. Inside, beneath neatly folded maintenance reports, lay an old brass spyglass his father had used. He drew it out, wiped the dust from its end, and extended it with one clean pull.

Through the spyglass, the light sharpened. It was still strange: not quite the yellow of flame, not quite the white of an electric bulb. It had an edge, a halo, like light seen through water. It hovered above the ocean’s skin, a few yards up, unsupported.

As he watched, it pulsed again: three short, three long, three short.

“Who are you?” he whispered.

No answer came, of course. Only the patient blink of distant brilliance. But under his palm, the foghorn lever twitched again, as if the very tower were taking a breath to shout.

This time, he did not hold it back.

“All right,” Elias said, and removed his hand.

The lever slammed down.

The horn’s cry tore through the room and out over the water, a blast of sound that made the glass shudder. It rolled away across the waves, diminishing, until it became something like a memory of thunder.

Far out on the horizon, the pale light steadied. It no longer blinked in code. It brightened, only slightly, but enough that he felt it, a tiny pressure at the base of his skull.

He had signaled hundreds of ships. He’d warned away captains drunk on bravado, guided trawlers home through murk, stood watch through gales that chewed on the rocks like bone. Never once had any of them answered the foghorn.

This one did.

The pale light flickered again, but not in human code. It strobed three times in rapid succession, then held, then dimmed. The pattern repeated, faster now, as if excited.

He realized, with a creeping chill, that the sound of the horn had not faded as much as it should have. It hung in the air, lingering in his ears, a low vibration that hummed in his teeth. It was not an echo. It was the call, still going, as though it had caught on something and was being drawn out into a long, impossible thread.

The tower vibrated around him, a faint tremor running through stone and steel. The lens chimed with tiny impacts as its prisms learned a new song.

“Enough,” he said sharply, and hauled the lever back up.

Silence fell in a sudden, intimate rush. The tower exhaled. The tremor stopped.

Out at sea, the light dimmed to its former pallor. For a heartbeat, Elias thought he saw it expand, like something taking form, and then it shrank again, coiling in upon itself.

He looked down at his hand. It shook.

This, he decided, would not go in the logbook. There were things you did not write down because ink made them too real. The Service would send a man in a suit, with questions and instruments, and they would tell him that atmospheric conditions and fatigue and old age were playing tricks.

He did not much mind being old, but he refused to be told his lighthouse was lying to him.

He folded the spyglass, slid it back into the drawer, and took one more long look at the light.

“Whatever you are,” he said quietly, “you stay out there. I’ll stay up here. That was always the bargain.”

The pale glow winked once, a brief, almost playful flare, then went out.

The horizon returned to its native emptiness.

Elias stayed in the lantern room until dawn, making his rounds more often than necessary, polishing the railing that did not need polishing, checking the bolts on mechanisms that had been sturdy for decades. He did not sleep, but he had gone long nights without sleep before. That, too, was part of the work.

The sun rose slow and grey over a calm sea. The glass warmed under its touch, and the last of the impossible dew dried away. As the light brightened, the memory of the pale glow felt thinner, like a dream already losing its color.

He could have convinced himself that it had been some trick of refraction, a distant yacht, a fishing boat with a new kind of lamp. He could have, perhaps, if not for the lever.

At seven in the morning, he went down to the office. The logbook waited.

He sat, opened it, and dipped his pen in ink. The nib hovered over the “Unusual Occurrence” column.

He thought of that long, stretched-out cry of the horn, the way it had pulled at the stones of the tower, at something in his chest. He thought of the pale light answering, eager and strange. He thought of the many nights his father had stared out at the same horizon, alone with his own unrecorded questions.

Elias wrote, in careful, blocky letters: Foghorn activated without input during clear weather. Light observed at sea responding to signal. Classification uncertain.

He paused, then added a final sentence: No immediate danger to navigation.

He closed the book and set the pen aside.

Later that week, the supply boat came, bringing fuel drums and mail and a new coil of rope. The young lad who ran it these days hopped up onto the dock with his usual boundless energy.

“You hear they’re talking of automating this place, Mr. Harper?” he called up, cupping his hands around his mouth.

Elias stood at the top of the stairs, wind tugging at his jacket. “They’ve been talking of that since I was your age.”

“This time they mean it, they say. All run by computers and such. No more keepers. Just lights that know what to do.”

Elias looked back over his shoulder at the tower, at the narrow windows, the stone that had watched tide after tide. Somewhere inside, the old gears sat patient, the lamp waiting for its night.

“Do they,” he said.

“Sure you don’t want to retire to the mainland?” the lad asked. “Must get lonely up there.”

Elias smiled, a slow, private thing. “There’s more company here than you’d think.”

He helped unload the fuel, signed the paperwork, accepted the letters he rarely answered. When the supply boat left, its wake stitched a brief white seam behind it, then vanished.

That night, he climbed the familiar stairs again, lit the lamp at dusk, and watched as the beam stretched out over the darkening sea. The horn lever rested in its housing, motionless and obedient.

Still, once the light settled into its steady sweep, Elias crossed to the bank of instruments and, very gently, laid his fingers on the iron arm.

“Just in case,” he said.

He stayed like that for a time, both hands resting on the old, cold metal, feeling the faint pulse of the mechanism, the even beat of his own heart, and somewhere beyond the glass and the waves, the possibility of something watching back.

The tower held its silence, bright and tall on the rocks. The sea rolled and hissed below. And in that narrow space between warning and answer, between duty and the things that would never fit in any logbook, the lighthouse keeper kept his watch.
